I do feel a bit tired sometimes, but I think that is just from all the stress of my upcoming retirement.\n\nDoctor: Since you weigh yourself every morning, could you share what the number on the scale was this morning, and also tell me how tall you are?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure of my exact height, and I would really rather not say the number on the scale from this morning. My doctor and my sisters say I'm too thin, but I shrug it off because I still see a little pouch on my stomach that I feel I need to lose. I don't know my exact height or weight numbers, but I weigh myself every morning and just focus on keeping that scale number from going up.\n\nDoctor: Since your doctor and sisters have mentioned you are too thin, did your doctor specifically state that your weight is medically underweight or dangerously low for your height?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure if my doctor used those exact words, to be honest. She and my sisters just kept saying I was \"too thin\" and she was worried about my low weight, but I didn't pay close attention to the specific medical terms because I still feel like I have weight to lose.\n\nDoctor: Are you still experiencing regular menstrual periods, or have they stopped or become irregular recently?\n\nPatient: Oh, I went through menopause many years ago since I am 64 now, so I don't get menstrual periods anymore. That stopped naturally for me quite a long time ago.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact numbers, could you give me a rough estimate of your height and about how much you weigh now, or how many pounds you have lost?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't know my exact height or weight numbers right now, and I can't really say how many pounds I've lost. I just know my uniforms are hanging off me and my wedding ring is spinning on my finger, though I shrug it off when others say I've lost too much.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact weight numbers, could you tell me what clothing size you used to wear before this weight loss started compared to what size you wear now?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure of the exact clothing sizes, but my clothes, especially my work uniforms, are now hanging very loosely off me. Even my wedding ring is constantly spinning on my finger because of how much smaller I've gotten.\n\nDoctor: Since losing weight, have you noticed any physical changes like feeling cold all the time, feeling dizzy when you stand up, or having very little energy?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed feeling cold or dizzy, to be honest. I do feel a bit tired sometimes, but I think that is just from all the stress of my upcoming retirement.\n\nDoctor: Since you weigh yourself every morning, could you share what the number on the scale was this morning, and also tell me how tall you are?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure of my exact height, and I would really rather not say the number on the scale from this morning. I get so anxious about the numbers going up that focusing on the specific weight just makes me feel worse.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned your Body Mass Index (BMI) number to you, specifically if it has dropped below 17.5?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor ever mentioning a specific BMI number or anything about 17.5. I just remember her expressing a lot of concern about my low weight and pointing out how loosely my clothes were hanging on me.\n\nDoctor: Since you've lost weight, have you noticed any other physical changes, such as your hair thinning or falling out, your skin becoming very dry, or fine downy hair starting to grow on your face or body?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really noticed any changes like that with my hair or my skin. Everything seems about the same as usual in those areas, so I haven't seen anything like thinning or new hair growth.\n\nDoctor: Apart from restricting your food, do you do anything else to keep your weight down, such as exercising excessively, making yourself throw up, or using laxatives or diet pills?\n\nPatient: No, I don't do any of those things like making myself throw up, taking pills, or exercising excessively. I only try to control my weight by being very careful about what I eat and keeping a close eye on the scale every morning.\n\nDoctor: To help me understand the severity of your weight loss, have you ever been hospitalized or required medical treatment specifically because your weight became dangerously low?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been hospitalized or needed any medical treatment for my weight before. This is the very first time my doctor has ever raised serious concerns about it and referred me to see someone.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever used terms like \"severely underweight,\" \"malnourished,\" or \"emaciated\" to describe your physical condition during your recent visits?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor using specific clinical terms like \"malnourished\" or \"emaciated\" during my visits. She did express a lot of concern about my low weight, though, and kept telling me that I was getting \"too thin.\"\n\nDoctor: Since you went through menopause years ago, we can't look at menstrual changes, but have you noticed a significant decrease in your sexual desire or interest in intimacy since your weight loss began?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about intimacy or sexual desire lately, to be honest. I just don't have the space in my head for anything else right now.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know your current weight, do you remember what your weight typically was before you started restricting your food?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't remember the exact number because I never really paid much attention to the scale back then. It is so different from now, where I feel like I am completely obsessed with checking the numbers every single morning.\n\nDoctor: Even if you prefer not to share the exact number on the scale, could you tell me if your weight is currently below 100 pounds?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure if it is below that specific number, and I prefer not to think about it in those terms. I just focus entirely on making sure the number on the scale doesn't go up when I step on it each morning.\n\nDoctor: Since your weight loss, has your doctor mentioned any concerns about your bone density, or have you been diagnosed with osteopenia or osteoporosis?\n\nPatient: No, my doctor hasn't mentioned anything about my bones or bone density. She has only expressed concern about my low weight, and before all this, she had just mentioned that my blood pressure and cholesterol were borderline.\n\nDoctor: Did your doctor or the nurse mention your actual weight during your last clinic visit, even if you tried not to look at the scale yourself?\n\nPatient: I don't recall the doctor or the nurse mentioning a specific weight number during the visit. They just expressed a lot of concern about me being \"too thin\" and having a \"low weight.\"\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor or anyone else recommended that you drink nutritional supplement shakes, like Ensure or Boost, or prescribed any specific treatment to help you gain weight?\n\nPatient: No, no one has recommended any supplement shakes or weight-gain treatments to me yet. My primary doctor was mostly just very worried about my low weight and decided to refer me here for this assessment instead. My family hasn't suggested anything like that either; they've just been constantly urging me to eat more.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned if your weight has dropped by 15% or more from what is considered normal for your height?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about the exact percentage, and I don't think my doctor ever mentioned 15% specifically. For example, do you strictly limit the amount of food you eat, or do you ever find yourself eating large amounts of food in a short period?\n\nPatient: I definitely don't eat large amounts; instead, I strictly limit myself to just picking at some yogurt or a few crackers, and I often tell my husband I already ate at work. I've completely cut out rice, pasteles, and anything with oil because I feel like those foods will go straight to my belly and make me huge.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced a significant drop in your weight recently, and could you share your current height and weight?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've lost enough weight that my work uniforms hang off me and my wedding ring just spins on my finger. My doctor and my sisters say I'm too thin, but I shrug it off because I still see a little pouch on my stomach that I feel I need to lose. I don't know my exact height or weight numbers, but I weigh myself every morning and just focus on keeping that scale number from going up.\n\nDoctor: Since your doctor and sisters have mentioned you are too thin, did your doctor specifically state that your weight is medically underweight or dangerously low for your height?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure if my doctor used those exact words, to be honest. She and my sisters just kept saying I was \"too thin\" and she was worried about my low weight, but I didn't pay close attention to the specific medical terms because I still feel like I have weight to lose.\n\nDoctor: Are you still experiencing regular menstrual periods, or have they stopped or become irregular recently?\n\nPatient: Oh, I went through menopause many years ago since I am 64 now, so I don't get menstrual periods anymore. That stopped naturally for me quite a long time ago.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact numbers, could you give me a rough estimate of your height and about how much you weigh now, or how many pounds you have lost?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't know my exact height or weight numbers right now, and I can't really say how many pounds I've lost. I just know my uniforms are hanging off me and my wedding ring is spinning on my finger, though I shrug it off when others say I've lost too much.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact weight numbers, could you tell me what clothing size you used to wear before this weight loss started compared to what size you wear now?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure of the exact clothing sizes, but my clothes, especially my work uniforms, are now hanging very loosely off me. Even my wedding ring is constantly spinning on my finger because of how much smaller I've gotten.\n\nDoctor: Since losing weight, have you noticed any physical changes like feeling cold all the time, feeling dizzy when you stand up, or having very little energy?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed feeling cold or dizzy, to be honest. I do feel a bit tired sometimes, but I think that is just from all the stress of my upcoming retirement.\n\nDoctor: Since you weigh yourself every morning, could you share what the number on the scale was this morning, and also tell me how tall you are?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure of my exact height, and I would really rather not say the number on the scale from this morning. I get so anxious about the numbers going up that focusing on the specific weight just makes me feel worse.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned your Body Mass Index (BMI) number to you, specifically if it has dropped below 17.5?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor ever mentioning a specific BMI number or anything about 17.5. I just remember her expressing a lot of concern about my low weight and pointing out how loosely my clothes were hanging on me.\n\nDoctor: Since you've lost weight, have you noticed any other physical changes, such as your hair thinning or falling out, your skin becoming very dry, or fine downy hair starting to grow on your face or body?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really noticed any changes like that with my hair or my skin. Everything seems about the same as usual in those areas, so I haven't seen anything like thinning or new hair growth.\n\nDoctor: Apart from restricting your food, do you do anything else to keep your weight down, such as exercising excessively, making yourself throw up, or using laxatives or diet pills?\n\nPatient: No, I don't do any of those things like making myself throw up, taking pills, or exercising excessively. I only try to control my weight by being very careful about what I eat and keeping a close eye on the scale every morning.\n\nDoctor: To help me understand the severity of your weight loss, have you ever been hospitalized or required medical treatment specifically because your weight became dangerously low?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been hospitalized or needed any medical treatment for my weight before. This is the very first time my doctor has ever raised serious concerns about it and referred me to see someone.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever used terms like \"severely underweight,\" \"malnourished,\" or \"emaciated\" to describe your physical condition during your recent visits?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor using specific clinical terms like \"malnourished\" or \"emaciated\" during my visits. She did express a lot of concern about my low weight, though, and kept telling me that I was getting \"too thin.\"\n\nDoctor: Since you went through menopause years ago, we can't look at menstrual changes, but have you noticed a significant decrease in your sexual desire or interest in intimacy since your weight loss began?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about intimacy or sexual desire lately, to be honest. My mind has been completely consumed by my weight, the food rules I've set, and all the anxiety I feel about my upcoming retirement. I just don't have the space in my head for anything else right now.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know your current weight, do you remember what your weight typically was before you started restricting your food?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't remember the exact number because I never really paid much attention to the scale back then. It is so different from now, where I feel like I am completely obsessed with checking the numbers every single morning.\n\nDoctor: Even if you prefer not to share the exact number on the scale, could you tell me if your weight is currently below 100 pounds?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure if it is below that specific number, and I prefer not to think about it in those terms. I just focus entirely on making sure the number on the scale doesn't go up when I step on it each morning.\n\nDoctor: Since your weight loss, has your doctor mentioned any concerns about your bone density, or have you been diagnosed with osteopenia or osteoporosis?\n\nPatient: No, my doctor hasn't mentioned anything about my bones or bone density. She has only expressed concern about my low weight, and before all this, she had just mentioned that my blood pressure and cholesterol were borderline.\n\nDoctor: Did your doctor or the nurse mention your actual weight during your last clinic visit, even if you tried not to look at the scale yourself?\n\nPatient: I don't recall the doctor or the nurse mentioning a specific weight number during the visit. They just expressed a lot of concern about me being \"too thin\" and having a \"low weight.\"\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor or anyone else recommended that you drink nutritional supplement shakes, like Ensure or Boost, or prescribed any specific treatment to help you gain weight?\n\nPatient: No, no one has recommended any supplement shakes or weight-gain treatments to me yet. My primary doctor was mostly just very worried about my low weight and decided to refer me here for this assessment instead. My family hasn't suggested anything like that either; they've just been constantly urging me to eat more.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned if your weight has dropped by 15% or more from what is considered normal for your height?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about the exact percentage, and I don't think my doctor ever mentioned 15% specifically. I just know that she and my sisters have told me I'm too thin and they are very concerned about my low weight.\n\nDoctor: To help me get a better picture, could you tell me roughly how tall you are? For example, are you around 5 feet, 5 feet 4 inches, or taller?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure of my exact height, and I haven't had it measured recently. I think I'm somewhere around average, but I honestly couldn't tell you the exact feet and inches.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a specific target weight, or a maximum weight that you absolutely refuse to go over?\n\nPatient: I don't have an exact number in mind for a target or maximum weight. I just feel this constant, overwhelming pressure to keep the number on the scale from going up at all.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned that you have an unusually slow heart rate or very low blood pressure during your recent checkups?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor ever mentioning a slow heart rate or very low blood pressure. She only mentioned that my blood pressure and cholesterol were \"borderline\" when I first started dieting.\n\nDoctor: When you were younger and still had your monthly periods, did you ever experience a time where your periods stopped for three months or more because of dieting or low weight?"
  }

I don't recall ever losing my period due to dieting when I was younger. These struggles with my eating and worrying about my weight are entirely new to me, and they only started recently as I approached retirement.

I've completely cut out rice, pasteles, and anything with oil because I feel like those foods will go straight to my belly and make me huge.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced a significant drop in your weight recently, and could you share your current height and weight?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've lost enough weight that my work uniforms hang off me and my wedding ring just spins on my finger. My doctor and my sisters say I'm too thin, but I shrug it off because I still see a little pouch on my stomach that I feel I need to lose. I don't know my exact height or weight numbers, but I weigh myself every morning and just focus on keeping that scale number from going up.\n\nDoctor: Since your doctor and sisters have mentioned you are too thin, did your doctor specifically state that your weight is medically underweight or dangerously low for your height?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure if my doctor used those exact words, to be honest. That stopped naturally for me quite a long time ago.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact numbers, could you give me a rough estimate of your height and about how much you weigh now, or how many pounds you have lost?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't know my exact height or weight numbers right now, and I can't really say how many pounds I've lost. I just know my uniforms are hanging off me and my wedding ring is spinning on my finger, though I shrug it off when others say I've lost too much.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact weight numbers, could you tell me what clothing size you used to wear before this weight loss started compared to what size you wear now?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure of the exact clothing sizes, but my clothes, especially my work uniforms, are now hanging very loosely off me. Even my wedding ring is constantly spinning on my finger because of how much smaller I've gotten.\n\nDoctor: Since losing weight, have you noticed any physical changes like feeling cold all the time, feeling dizzy when you stand up, or having very little energy?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed feeling cold or dizzy, to be honest. I do feel a bit tired sometimes, but I think that is just from all the stress of my upcoming retirement.\n\nDoctor: Since you weigh yourself every morning, could you share what the number on the scale was this morning, and also tell me how tall you are?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure of my exact height, and I would really rather not say the number on the scale from this morning. I get so anxious about the numbers going up that focusing on the specific weight just makes me feel worse.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned your Body Mass Index (BMI) number to you, specifically if it has dropped below 17.5?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor ever mentioning a specific BMI number or anything about 17.5. I just remember her expressing a lot of concern about my low weight and pointing out how loosely my clothes were hanging on me.\n\nDoctor: Since you've lost weight, have you noticed any other physical changes, such as your hair thinning or falling out, your skin becoming very dry, or fine downy hair starting to grow on your face or body?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really noticed any changes like that with my hair or my skin. Everything seems about the same as usual in those areas, so I haven't seen anything like thinning or new hair growth.\n\nDoctor: Apart from restricting your food, do you do anything else to keep your weight down, such as exercising excessively, making yourself throw up, or using laxatives or diet pills?\n\nPatient: No, I don't do any of those things like making myself throw up, taking pills, or exercising excessively. I only try to control my weight by being very careful about what I eat and keeping a close eye on the scale every morning.\n\nDoctor: To help me understand the severity of your weight loss, have you ever been hospitalized or required medical treatment specifically because your weight became dangerously low?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been hospitalized or needed any medical treatment for my weight before. This is the very first time my doctor has ever raised serious concerns about it and referred me to see someone.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever used terms like \"severely underweight,\" \"malnourished,\" or \"emaciated\" to describe your physical condition during your recent visits?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor using specific clinical terms like \"malnourished\" or \"emaciated\" during my visits. She did express a lot of concern about my low weight, though, and kept telling me that I was getting \"too thin.\"\n\nDoctor: Since you went through menopause years ago, we can't look at menstrual changes, but have you noticed a significant decrease in your sexual desire or interest in intimacy since your weight loss began?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about intimacy or sexual desire lately, to be honest. My mind has been completely consumed by my weight, the food rules I've set, and all the anxiety I feel about my upcoming retirement. I just don't have the space in my head for anything else right now.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know your current weight, do you remember what your weight typically was before you started restricting your food?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't remember the exact number because I never really paid much attention to the scale back then. I just focus entirely on making sure the number on the scale doesn't go up when I step on it each morning.\n\nDoctor: Since your weight loss, has your doctor mentioned any concerns about your bone density, or have you been diagnosed with osteopenia or osteoporosis?\n\nPatient: No, my doctor hasn't mentioned anything about my bones or bone density. She has only expressed concern about my low weight, and before all this, she had just mentioned that my blood pressure and cholesterol were borderline.\n\nDoctor: Did your doctor or the nurse mention your actual weight during your last clinic visit, even if you tried not to look at the scale yourself?\n\nPatient: I don't recall the doctor or the nurse mentioning a specific weight number during the visit. They just expressed a lot of concern about me being \"too thin\" and having a \"low weight.\"\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor or anyone else recommended that you drink nutritional supplement shakes, like Ensure or Boost, or prescribed any specific treatment to help you gain weight?\n\nPatient: No, no one has recommended any supplement shakes or weight-gain treatments to me yet. My primary doctor was mostly just very worried about my low weight and decided to refer me here for this assessment instead. My family hasn't suggested anything like that either; they've just been constantly urging me to eat more.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned if your weight has dropped by 15% or more from what is considered normal for your height?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about the exact percentage, and I don't think my doctor ever mentioned 15% specifically. I just know that she and my sisters have told me I'm too thin and they are very concerned about my low weight.\n\nDoctor: To help me get a better picture, could you tell me roughly how tall you are? For example, are you around 5 feet, 5 feet 4 inches, or taller?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure of my exact height, and I haven't had it measured recently. I think I'm somewhere around average, but I honestly couldn't tell you the exact feet and inches.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a specific target weight, or a maximum weight that you absolutely refuse to go over?\n\nPatient: I don't have an exact number in mind for a target or maximum weight. I just feel this constant, overwhelming pressure to keep the number on the scale from going up at all.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned that you have an unusually slow heart rate or very low blood pressure during your recent checkups?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor ever mentioning a slow heart rate or very low blood pressure. These struggles with my eating and worrying about my weight are entirely new to me, and they only started recently as I approached retirement.\n\nDoctor: Do you know if your doctor wrote \"anorexia nervosa\" or a similar eating disorder diagnosis on your referral paperwork or medical chart?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure exactly what was written on the referral paperwork. That stopped naturally for me quite a long time ago.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact numbers, could you give me a rough estimate of your height and about how much you weigh now, or how many pounds you have lost?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't know my exact height or weight numbers right now, and I can't really say how many pounds I've lost. I just know my uniforms are hanging off me and my wedding ring is spinning on my finger, though I shrug it off when others say I've lost too much.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know the exact weight numbers, could you tell me what clothing size you used to wear before this weight loss started compared to what size you wear now?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure of the exact clothing sizes, but my clothes, especially my work uniforms, are now hanging very loosely off me. Even my wedding ring is constantly spinning on my finger because of how much smaller I've gotten.\n\nDoctor: Since losing weight, have you noticed any physical changes like feeling cold all the time, feeling dizzy when you stand up, or having very little energy?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed feeling cold or dizzy, to be honest. I do feel a bit tired sometimes, but I think that is just from all the stress of my upcoming retirement.\n\nDoctor: Since you weigh yourself every morning, could you share what the number on the scale was this morning, and also tell me how tall you are?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure of my exact height, and I would really rather not say the number on the scale from this morning. I get so anxious about the numbers going up that focusing on the specific weight just makes me feel worse.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned your Body Mass Index (BMI) number to you, specifically if it has dropped below 17.5?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor ever mentioning a specific BMI number or anything about 17.5. I just remember her expressing a lot of concern about my low weight and pointing out how loosely my clothes were hanging on me.\n\nDoctor: Since you've lost weight, have you noticed any other physical changes, such as your hair thinning or falling out, your skin becoming very dry, or fine downy hair starting to grow on your face or body?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really noticed any changes like that with my hair or my skin. Everything seems about the same as usual in those areas, so I haven't seen anything like thinning or new hair growth.\n\nDoctor: Apart from restricting your food, do you do anything else to keep your weight down, such as exercising excessively, making yourself throw up, or using laxatives or diet pills?\n\nPatient: No, I don't do any of those things like making myself throw up, taking pills, or exercising excessively. I only try to control my weight by being very careful about what I eat and keeping a close eye on the scale every morning.\n\nDoctor: To help me understand the severity of your weight loss, have you ever been hospitalized or required medical treatment specifically because your weight became dangerously low?\n\nPatient: No, I have never been hospitalized or needed any medical treatment for my weight before. This is the very first time my doctor has ever raised serious concerns about it and referred me to see someone.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever used terms like \"severely underweight,\" \"malnourished,\" or \"emaciated\" to describe your physical condition during your recent visits?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor using specific clinical terms like \"malnourished\" or \"emaciated\" during my visits. She did express a lot of concern about my low weight, though, and kept telling me that I was getting \"too thin.\"\n\nDoctor: Since you went through menopause years ago, we can't look at menstrual changes, but have you noticed a significant decrease in your sexual desire or interest in intimacy since your weight loss began?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about intimacy or sexual desire lately, to be honest. My mind has been completely consumed by my weight, the food rules I've set, and all the anxiety I feel about my upcoming retirement. I just don't have the space in my head for anything else right now.\n\nDoctor: Even if you don't know your current weight, do you remember what your weight typically was before you started restricting your food?\n\nPatient: I honestly don't remember the exact number because I never really paid much attention to the scale back then. It is so different from now, where I feel like I am completely obsessed with checking the numbers every single morning.\n\nDoctor: Even if you prefer not to share the exact number on the scale, could you tell me if your weight is currently below 100 pounds?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure if it is below that specific number, and I prefer not to think about it in those terms. I just focus entirely on making sure the number on the scale doesn't go up when I step on it each morning.\n\nDoctor: Since your weight loss, has your doctor mentioned any concerns about your bone density, or have you been diagnosed with osteopenia or osteoporosis?\n\nPatient: No, my doctor hasn't mentioned anything about my bones or bone density. She has only expressed concern about my low weight, and before all this, she had just mentioned that my blood pressure and cholesterol were borderline.\n\nDoctor: Did your doctor or the nurse mention your actual weight during your last clinic visit, even if you tried not to look at the scale yourself?\n\nPatient: I don't recall the doctor or the nurse mentioning a specific weight number during the visit. They just expressed a lot of concern about me being \"too thin\" and having a \"low weight.\"\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor or anyone else recommended that you drink nutritional supplement shakes, like Ensure or Boost, or prescribed any specific treatment to help you gain weight?\n\nPatient: No, no one has recommended any supplement shakes or weight-gain treatments to me yet. My primary doctor was mostly just very worried about my low weight and decided to refer me here for this assessment instead. My family hasn't suggested anything like that either; they've just been constantly urging me to eat more.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned if your weight has dropped by 15% or more from what is considered normal for your height?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about the exact percentage, and I don't think my doctor ever mentioned 15% specifically. I just know that she and my sisters have told me I'm too thin and they are very concerned about my low weight.\n\nDoctor: To help me get a better picture, could you tell me roughly how tall you are? For example, are you around 5 feet, 5 feet 4 inches, or taller?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure of my exact height, and I haven't had it measured recently. I think I'm somewhere around average, but I honestly couldn't tell you the exact feet and inches.\n\nDoctor: Do you have a specific target weight, or a maximum weight that you absolutely refuse to go over?\n\nPatient: I don't have an exact number in mind for a target or maximum weight. I just feel this constant, overwhelming pressure to keep the number on the scale from going up at all.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever mentioned that you have an unusually slow heart rate or very low blood pressure during your recent checkups?\n\nPatient: I don't recall my doctor ever mentioning a slow heart rate or very low blood pressure. She only mentioned that my blood pressure and cholesterol were \"borderline\" when I first started dieting.\n\nDoctor: When you were younger and still had your monthly periods, did you ever experience a time where your periods stopped for three months or more because of dieting or low weight?\n\nPatient: I don't recall ever losing my period due to dieting when I was younger. These struggles with my eating and worrying about my weight are entirely new to me, and they only started recently as I approached retirement.\n\nDoctor: Do you know if your doctor wrote \"anorexia nervosa\" or a similar eating disorder diagnosis on your referral paperwork or medical chart?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure exactly what was written on the referral paperwork. I just know that my doctor was very worried about my weight and referred me to a specialist to get checked out.\n\nDoctor: Do you know if your current weight is considered medically underweight, or is it still within the normal range for your height?\n\nPatient: My primary doctor and my sisters have told me that I am too thin and expressed a lot of concern about my low weight, so it might be. But I personally shrug it off because when I look in the mirror, I still see a little pouch on my stomach and feel like I actually need to lose more weight before I stop.\n\nDoctor: Before you began restricting your food, had your doctor ever told you that you were overweight or recommended that you lose weight for your health?"
